extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents, and patent office examiners operating in ASEAN Member States (AMS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for prosecution, examination, publication, amendment, and related procedural requirements for patent applications in ASEAN Member States. Covers examiner practices, applicant options, timing, and substantive patentability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments must not introduce new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant amendments (including amendments filed before grant or after formalities examination) must not result in the application including subject-matter extending beyond that disclosed in the application as originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may be informed by the patent office/Registrar during substantive examination if amendment(s) filed constitute new matter and will be allowed to amend them within a prescribed period. An amendment is unallowable as new matter if the overall change results in information not directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed; however, an applicant may be allowed to introduce matter if it is a convincing obvious clarification to a person skilled in the art. Requests to limit an already-allowable claim or to improve clarity are normally allowed. Consider unity and alignment between description and claims when claims have been substantially limited. Applicants are not generally required to re-publish amended applications (exception: Viet Nam). Singapore makes amendments available on the dossier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-formalities amendment conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may request amendment of the specification after completion of the formalities examination, provided the amendment does not add subject-matter beyond the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies in all AMS; applicants must comply with pre-grant amendment limits and will be subject to the same new-matter tests described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing medium for amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments can be filed electronically or on paper, except where national rules require electronic filing only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singapore only allows amendments filed electronically. Other AMS permit either medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment uses a priori and a posteriori approaches. The link must be a technical relationship expressed in the claims as the same or corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity must be determined from the language of the claims properly construed and, where appropriate, having regard to relevant prior art. Lack of unity may be evident a priori (from claims alone) or a posteriori (after considering prior art). The unity assessment should ensure efficient use of examination resources and be considered early. Do not raise or maintain a lack of unity objection on a narrow or literal approach; take a broad, practical view of interdependence in light of the state of the art. Example: independent claims A+Z, A+Y, Z+Y lack unity a priori if no subject-matter common to all three; A+Z and A+Y have unity a priori because A is common, but A being known in the prior art can cause lack of unity a posteriori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If unity is lacking, applicant may be required to limit claims or may file divisional application(s) which must not contain subject-matter beyond the initial application's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether divisionals may be filed proactively or only after objection varies by AMS (except Myanmar and Thailand, most allow both). Claims of a divisional need not be limited to subject-matter already claimed in the parent to avoid double patenting issues. Divisionals retain the filing date and priority of the parent and multiple nested divisionals are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing licence requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS require obtaining a foreign filing licence before filing abroad; requirements vary by country (residency-based or based on where inventive activity occurred and/or citizenship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five AMS (Brunei, Malaysia, Myanmar, Singapore, Viet Nam) have foreign filing licence requirements with different triggers; failure to adhere can have penalties. In some jurisdictions the requirement applies only to inventions affecting national security/public order. Obtaining a licence should be simple and expeditive, typically requiring a petition, fee (if applicable), and copies of relevant documents. Other AMS without formal licences may have prohibitions on inventions that endanger national security/public order/morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordal of change of name/address
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes of name and/or address of applicant or inventor can be recorded during formalities examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes must be entered in the Register and are typically supported by documentary evidence; documents are checked for appropriate form and fee payment and recorded with date of receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal before formalities and publication consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent application is withdrawn before formalities examination starts, in most AMS it will not be published (exception: the Philippines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-publication on withdrawal allows refiling without facing a novelty objection in most AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rejection/abandonment of priority application
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection or abandonment of a priority application does not automatically cause rejection of a corresponding patent application claiming priority from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care is required where the reasons for abandonment/rejection reveal potentially relevant earlier disclosures by the same applicant (or predecessor in title) that constitute prior art and could undermine the later application's patentability. In such cases, rejection of the priority application may lead to rejection of the subsequent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative and judicial appeal of formality decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request administrative relief against decisions/orders of the patent office/Registrar and may appeal to the courts where provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All AMS provide administrative relief; all permit judicial appeal (Brunei Darussalam has limits on court appeal for some Registrar decisions). If a refusal is reversed on appeal, the examiner is bound by the court decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and legal effect of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of a patent application in the official journal/gazette (paper or electronic) serves to make the application prior art, enable public monitoring and filings of observations/oppositions/revocations, and, in some AMS, triggers provisional protection and liability for damages from the publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, pending applications do not create infringement liability, but certain AMS provide provisional protection and claim to damages from publication—see national provisions (Paragraph 3.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for publication of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications are published as soon as possible after 18 months from the filing date or priority date, unless withdrawn, deemed withdrawn, or refused before publication preparations are completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 18-month standard applies in Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Viet Nam. Applicants are notified of publication in most AMS except Singapore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delaying or expediting publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request deferment of publication or early publication in certain AMS subject to national rules and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deferment of publication by request is available only in Thailand. Early publication may be requested in most AMS, but Lao PDR, Malaysia, and Thailand excepted. Some AMS require reasons (e.g., Indonesia), others do not (Brunei, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore). Indonesia and the Philippines limit early publication not earlier than six months from filing. Advantages include faster prosecution and earlier claim to infringement damages. Failure to meet publication requirements may lead to denial of an early publication request but usually will not cause withdrawal of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of patent gazette/bulletin publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication must include title, description, claims, most representative drawings filed (if any), any sequence listing filed at filing date, late-filed missing parts (if not withdrawn and not introducing new matter), applicant name/address, inventor(s), patent agent (if any), priority application number/date (if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments that introduced new matter outside the disclosure as filed are not included in publication. Specific contents published vary by AMS and are detailed in CSR Annexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of claims of published applications (pre-grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amending claims of a published patent application before grant is normal but amendments must not introduce subject-matter extending beyond the initial application's disclosure and must not create clarity issues or other objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An amendment is unallowable if the overall content change is not directly and unambiguously derivable by the person skilled in the art. Obvious clarifications in context may be permitted. A request to limit an already allowable claim, or to improve clarity, is normally allowed. Substantial claim limitation raises special considerations: unity of invention and alignment between description and claims. Re-publication after amendment is not generally required (except Viet Nam); Singapore posts amendments to the dossier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of granted patent specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Granted patent specifications are published (all AMS except Cambodia; Singapore publishes only a reference to grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final publication includes the granted claims, description and drawings, enabling clear assessment of granted rights for licensing, enforcement and freedom-to-operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction and (re-)publication for clerical/obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent proprietors may apply to correct clerical errors or obvious mistakes in granted patents subject to conditions and fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications should be accompanied by a statement/declaration explaining the facts and why discretion should be exercised. Clerical error defined as mistake in process (e.g., word processing) distinct from lack of knowledge. Obvious mistake must be evident from the documents as a whole that an error occurred and what correction is needed. Singapore may publish the correction for opposition and then apply it; most AMS (except Philippines and Viet Nam) do not re-publish corrected specifications. Singapore records corrections in the register/dossier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration, format and languages of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Format (paper/electronic) and languages of patent publication vary by AMS; some publish only electronically, others in both formats; duration of publication may be specified in national provisions or left to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Viet Nam publish in both paper and electronic form; Brunei, Lao PDR, Philippines, Singapore electronic only. Cambodia copies made available on payment. Duration is specified in some AMS (Brunei, Indonesia) and not fixed in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion between patent and petty patent/utility model
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion of a patent application into a petty patent/simple patent/utility model (and vice versa) is possible under national conditions and timing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion is commonly used when prior art undermines inventive step. Timing windows vary: up to grant/refusal in some AMS, before publication in Thailand, before substantive examination in Lao PDR, within six months of substantive exam report in Malaysia. The converted application is published under the applicable petty-patent/utility-model publication conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rights/liability upon publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS provide applicants with provisional rights upon publication, allowing applicants to send warning letters and potentially claim damages from publication date under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority of AMS (Brunei, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Viet Nam) provide provisional rights in accordance with Section 3.9 of the CSR; applicants may notify alleged infringers of filing/publication date and demand cessation of infringing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination purpose and scope (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive examination involves prior art search and assessment of patentability: novelty, inventive step, industrial application, excluded subject-matter, sufficiency (enablement), clarity of claims, unity of invention, and that amendments do not go beyond original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objections are raised, examiners invite applicants to amend and/or explain; if objections are overcome a patent is granted, otherwise refused. Most AMS conduct search and examination directly; some outsource search/examination to other capable offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits to request substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive examination must commence within prescribed national time limits which vary across AMS and may be between 18 and 60 months from specified events (publication date, international filing date, national filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In jurisdictions where substantive examination does not start automatically, applicants must file a formal request within the timeline prescribed in CSR 4.2; failure to file may result in deemed withdrawal. Examples: Philippines 18 months, Thailand up to 60 months. IP5 offices commonly allow requests up to 18-36 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PCT work products in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent offices may utilise PCT international search reports, written opinions and International Preliminary Reports on Patentability as work products to assist national substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These PCT reports, while not binding, are translated into English and provided in standard format and can increase likelihood of granting high-quality patents by international cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified examination relying on foreign granted patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS allow replacement of part or all of national search/examination by evidence that equivalent work has been done by a recognised foreign patent office (e.g., amendment to match granted specification and evidence of grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must be amended to be substantially the same as the specification and claims of the granted counterpart and evidence of the granted patent filed; the local examiner will then examine the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and bilateral sharing of search and examination work products
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS participate in regional frameworks (ASPEC) and bilateral arrangements to share and use search/examination reports to support national examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under ASPEC most AMS (except Myanmar) allow sharing. Bilateral frameworks exist with offices such as the EPO and JPO. Offices may also unilaterally use foreign work products and may require applicants to submit information about corresponding foreign applications/grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of prior art information by applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no formal requirement in AMS for applicants to submit known prior art at filing or to continuously supply newly-discovered prior art during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some national practices may permit or request such submissions, but generally applicants are not mandated to proactively provide prior art beyond what is required by national procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party observations (TPO) mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may submit observations (prior art) to examiners in some AMS (e.g., Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore) to assist examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party observations are typically included in the file and do not trigger inter partes procedures; examiners may take them into account. Submission windows: Malaysia within 3 months of publication (with fee); Philippines within 6 months (with fee); Singapore anytime between publication and issuance of relevant exam report. EPO-style online systems allow submissions at any time. Submitted prior art, even if unused by examiner, may be used by others later to challenge validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsourcing substantive examination to external experts/offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices with limited resources may carry out search/examination fully or partly in cooperation with other patent offices or external technical experts while retaining autonomy to decide grant/refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate confidentiality measures (e.g., contractual frameworks) must be taken to maintain dossier confidentiality when outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant choice regarding which office conducts substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants generally do not have the option to choose between local substantive examination and substantive examination conducted by a foreign patent office; choice may be available only for searches in some AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a few AMS (e.g., Thailand) applicants may select an office to conduct the search, but substantive examination remains governed by national procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination includes determination of whether claimed subject-matter is excluded from patentable subject matter (e.g., abstract theories, discoveries, methods of treatment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of excluded subject-matter are complex and are typically handled during substantive examination by examiners experienced in patentability conditions; see Chapter 5 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination assesses whether the application relates to only one invention or to a group forming a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further details and procedures for dealing with lack of unity are provided in Chapter 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — clarity of invention (claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of the application, especially the claims, is vital; meaning of claim terms should be clear to the person skilled in the art from the claim wording alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity affects assessment of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; see Chapter 7 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — sufficient disclosure (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must provide sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the art to practise the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement assessments ensure the invention can be carried out; see Chapter 8 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is required: the invention must be new and not publicly known or in public use by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty assessment looks to prior public disclosures; see Chapter 10 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — inventive step (non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must involve an inventive step; it must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art with regard to prior art on the effective filing/priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step analysis is jurisdiction-dependent; see Chapter 11 for methodology and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of substantive examination — industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can only be granted for an invention capable of industrial application (can be made or used in some kind of industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial applicability is assessed per national law; see Chapter 12 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for expediting substantive examination (PPH and regional programmes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may accelerate examination via Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) bilateral programmes, regional PPH (ASPEC) programmes, PCT-ASPEC, and national/bilateral acceleration schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under PPH, if corresponding claims are found patentable by an earlier office, applicants may request accelerated examination at the later office which can use prior work product. Regional ASPEC programmes and national fast-track schemes (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore) have specific eligibility criteria, caps, fees, tech-field restrictions and procedural conditions (e.g., applicant reasons, claim caps, entity caps). National programmes may impose additional conditions, response deadlines, and expected grant timelines (examples provided for Thailand, Singapore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of patentability during formality vs substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability assessments are generally conducted during substantive examination (exception: Viet Nam conducts assessment in both formality and substantive stages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patentability assessment is complex, it is recommended to perform it during substantive examination by examiners experienced in patentability matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of substantive examination reports to third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive examination reports should be made available to third parties at the latest after the granting date of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making examination reports available supports transparency and third-party evaluation of patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to respond and appeal substantive examination decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must be allowed to respond to objections raised in substantive examination reports and may appeal rejections through administrative and judicial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses may include explanations, data or evidence; whether a response is admitted depends on the case. If the examiner upholds rejection, appeals to upper administrative bodies or competent courts are available; procedures and grounds for appeal are jurisdiction-specific.
